claims.title: Unauthenticated settlement callbacks can falsely mark orders paid
claims.description: `flow:entity:card-processor>process:storefront-api>settlement-webhook` crosses from the public internet to the internet-facing `process:storefront-api`, while its `authentication` state is unknown. If callback authentication is not enforced, an outside attacker can forge a settlement confirmation on that flow so `process:storefront-api` marks an order paid without a genuine processor callback. This is conditional on resolving the webhook authentication gap; it does not assert that authentication is absent.

quotes.text: I would have to check how that callback is authenticated.

severity.justification: Likelihood is medium and conditional because `process:storefront-api` is internet-facing and the webhook crosses the public-internet boundary, but `authentication` is unverified rather than stated absent. Impact is medium because the flow carries financial settlement status and the described action changes whether an order is treated as paid.

mitigations.detail: Require verification of a processor-specific signature or mTLS identity on `flow:entity:card-processor>process:storefront-api>settlement-webhook`, rejecting callbacks that do not authenticate as the processor.

mitigations.summary: Bind callbacks to expected payment state
mitigations.detail: Validate the order identifier, expected amount, processor transaction identifier, and permitted payment-state transition before `process:storefront-api` marks an order paid; retain replay-resistant delivery identifiers.

claims.title: A compromised storefront API can forge orders accepted by the core service
claims.description: `flow:process:storefront-api>process:order-service>submit-order` crosses into the core-services zone, and `process:order-service` accepts submissions without authentication. An attacker controlling `process:storefront-api` can forge or alter order submissions on that flow, including shopper identifiers and shipping addresses, and `process:order-service` will process them as accepted work. Second-order, the order service persists the fabricated order data through `flow:process:order-service>store:orders-db>read-write-orders` and writes a receipt through `flow:process:order-service>store:receipt-archive>append-receipt`.

quotes.text: Orders, shopper addresses and card-last-four live in a PostgreSQL database (orders-db) that the order service reads and writes with a single application account that has full read/write.

severity.justification: Likelihood is medium: exploiting the unauthenticated core-service operation requires control of `process:storefront-api` or another way to reach the internal service, but the order-service authorization grant accepts anything that does reach it. Impact is high because forged orders are persisted with shopper addresses and payment-related card-last-four data and can produce authoritative receipts.

mitigations.summary: Require workload authentication for order submission
mitigations.detail: Require mTLS or workload identity on `flow:process:storefront-api>process:order-service>submit-order` and authorize only the storefront API identity to submit orders.

mitigations.summary: Bind orders to validated storefront context
mitigations.detail: Have `process:order-service` verify a signed, short-lived order submission context and enforce server-side validation of shopper and order fields before persistence.

claims.title: A stolen application-account password enables direct order-record modification
claims.description: The application account used on `flow:process:order-service>store:orders-db>read-write-orders` has full read/write authority, and its password is held in an environment variable on `process:order-service`. An attacker who obtains that static credential can alter rows directly in `store:orders-db`, bypassing order-service validation and rewriting orders, shipping addresses, or card-last-four-associated records. Second-order, `process:order-service` reads the altered records through the same read-write flow and can act on corrupted order state.

quotes.text: The password comes from an environment variable on the worker.

severity.justification: Likelihood is medium because an attacker must first obtain the static application-account password, but the credential is retained in the worker environment and is immediately usable. Impact is high because the account has full read/write access to `store:orders-db`, which holds orders, shopper addresses, and card-last-four data.

mitigations.summary: Replace the static database password with workload identity
mitigations.detail: Use short-lived workload-federated database credentials for `process:order-service` rather than a long-lived password in its environment.
Replace the application account's blanket full read/write grant with least-privilege roles limited to the tables and operations required by the order service.
Restrict direct database access to approved service paths and alert on writes not attributable to the order-service workload identity.

claims.title: Unverified encryption at rest leaves orders-db vulnerable to offline record tampering
claims.description: `store:orders-db` has `encryption_at_rest` state unknown while holding orders, shopper addresses, and card-last-four data. If the unresolved control means backups, snapshots, or other storage copies are not protected with authenticated encryption and restore-integrity checks, an attacker holding such a copy can alter order records and have corrupted data restored into `store:orders-db`. `process:order-service` then consumes the tampered state through `flow:process:order-service>store:orders-db>read-write-orders`. This is conditional on the unknown storage-encryption state and does not claim that encryption is absent.

quotes.text: Orders, shopper addresses and card-last-four live in a PostgreSQL database (orders-db)

severity.justification: Likelihood is low and conditional: exploitation requires an attacker to obtain an offline orders-db copy and the unknown encryption control to prove ineffective or absent. Impact is high because altered database records affect orders and the store holds shopper addresses and payment-related card-last-four data.

mitigations.summary: Verify encryption and integrity protection for all orders-db copies
mitigations.detail: Establish whether `store:orders-db`, its backups, and snapshots use managed authenticated encryption with controlled keys; enforce it for every copy.

mitigations.summary: Validate database restores before production use
mitigations.detail: Require signed backup manifests, integrity verification, and controlled restore approval so altered snapshots cannot be accepted as authentic order data.

claims.title: Conflicting receipt-archive encryption statements leave offline receipt tampering unresolved
claims.description: The model states absent encryption at rest for `store:receipt-archive`, while the source-derived storage-encryption assertion records a conflicting customer-managed-key statement. If the discrepancy resolves to an unprotected or unverifiable archive copy, an attacker with a storage copy can alter receipt objects before they are restored or otherwise accepted as archive content. That changes business-critical receipt records that purport to record completed orders and the order-service write. This is a conditional finding about the unresolved storage-encryption conflict, not an assertion that the bucket lacks encryption.

quotes.text: the bucket is encrypted with a customer-managed key.

severity.justification: Likelihood is low and conditional because an attacker must obtain an offline archive copy and the conflicting storage-encryption statements must resolve to ineffective protection. Impact is medium because `store:receipt-archive` holds business-critical receipt records whose integrity supports completed-order evidence.

mitigations.summary: Resolve and enforce the receipt-archive encryption configuration
mitigations.detail: Reconcile the model with the stated customer-managed-key configuration and verify that encryption covers every receipt object, version, backup, and export.
Maintain signed object manifests or immutable versioning and validate them during recovery so modified archived receipts cannot be restored as legitimate records.
